blocks.text: Water drips somewhere in the dark. Onto stone. Slow and regular, like a tell-weight with nobody holding it.

The Wellhead Drum sweats. I feel it through my soles before the Warden has finished his first word: every stand furred with wet, the grain closed up tight and cold as a cellar step in February. My toes curl on their own.
"Pace five," says the Warden.
That's all he has to tell us, and he only has to tell us once a Half. Whatever the floor does after that, nobody announces.
Tonight this floor is going to change under us halfway through. Nobody is going to say so. I'll be the only one who feels it, and I won't know what I'm feeling.
Three hours earlier, I was dry.
The carrier's cart to Wellhead smells of turnips and of the man who owns the turnips. Sef sits on a sack facing backwards, so he can talk to all of us and none of the road.

I sit facing forwards with my boots on, laced tight. On our kiln stair after Round Three, Callista Veyne told me she'd watched my feet. I didn't answer her. I put my boots on in front of her and walked home. All week I've laced them like someone's watching.
"Three things," says Sef. "One. I went to Tannery last night."
"On purpose?" says Dov.

"Two. The Tannery Hounds. Unbeaten, top of the Run, and they throw low. Only low. Two bass Callers. I'm calling them Thunder and Worse. Three, they throw slow, all night, never hurry." He looks at his fingers and puts up another one, annoyed with it. "Four things. Four, Wren can't touch them."
"I can touch anything," I say. "I'm a mason. I touch things for a living."
"Not with a pair, you can't."
"Wren Halloway," says Mrs. Oduya, from the good side of the cart, the side with the blanket. "Consider a stockpot."
"I'd rather not. I've had no breakfast."

"A kettle is quick," she says, as if I hadn't spoken. "Small water, high note, short wave. A stockpot is slow. A low note is a long note. At pace five, I should think Thunder's notes run six paces crest to crest. Worse, seven."
I do it in stone. A pair stands half a wave apart along the beam, and never more than two and a half paces apart. Half of seven is three and a half.
"So nothing longer than five," I say.
"Nothing longer than five paces, on any floor in Caddrow," says Mrs. Oduya. "It is a matter of arithmetic."
"So against Tannery," says Sef, "we're two Dampers again. Plain ones. Everything that reaches us goes in, and into the Book."
Marten, wedged between two sacks with his knees up, nods slowly. "Aye, well."
"Tannery's not today," says Dov. "Today's Wellhead. Can we lose one thing at a time?"

I count the tin in my head while the cart grinds up Pump Hill. Four crowns. Wellhead's an away match, so there's no gate for us, only the walk back. Four of thirty-eight. Thirty-four to find, and Midwinter Quarter Day doesn't move for anybody.

The Wellhead Drum is under an old well-house at the back of a pump yard, and it smells like the bottom of a bucket. The stair is slick. The walls are slick. Bare-footed, I can feel the whole place breathing out cold, the way a church does in August.

Mrs. Oduya goes to the plate rail, gets a nod from the Warden, and taps the nearest plate with one knuckle. Then the next. She tilts her head, listens, and frowns. I've never seen her frown at a plate before. She frowns at Dov, often. Plates, never.
"What?" I say. "Is it cracked?"
"Nothing is wrong with them." She taps a third. "They are sporting plates."
"As opposed to?"

"As opposed to ours." She lays a palm flat on the brass to still it. "The Kilnyard plates are cast in a speaking scale. Not a sporting one. The steps between them are intervals no sport needs. And our Last Plate rests on the Calling Tone."
Sef's pencil stops. He doesn't look down at it; he never does. "What's a speaking scale?"
"How do you know that?" I ask.
Mrs. Oduya looks at me for a moment, very kindly.
"Sefton Brask," she says, "your collar is folded under. Wren Halloway, your feet are blue." And she walks off down the rail to find our Last Plate's peg.
Dov watches her go with his mouth open. "She changed the subject."
"She's allowed."
"She doesn't change subjects. She finishes them. She buries them and plants roses."
Across the floor, Wellhead are warming up in oilskins. Sef stands at my right shoulder and runs them.

"Two things. One, their Callers. The thin one with the cough, Hesketh Moon. I'm calling him the Drip. The woman who smiles at everything is Grin. Two Callers, no Tuner. Two, they've played eleven years in this sweat, and they look happy about it. I don't like that."
"Neither do I."
The Warden swings his tell-weight, announces his pace, and the wet starts dripping somewhere in the dark again.
First Half, the Drip's first Raise.

His lead-in comes up through my soles a beat before it could ever cross the air: clean, mid-high, two hand-widths over our peg. I learned Wellhead's floor chart on the cart, tapping it out on a turnip sack. For that pitch at pace five there's a pair: Marten's stand and the one beside the drain, a pace and three-tenths apart along the Drip's line.
"Marten. Drain side."
I step. He sets. I turn to face him and make my mouth big.
"Three. Two. Draw."
The front crawls in, glowing faintly, slow as a man crossing a room, and we draw together, and the note dies in the wet air between us like a candle pinched out.
The Warden puts his rod's foot to my stand, then to Marten's. "Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
I stand still afterwards and wait. I don't mean to. My feet just do it. At home, after the first one, three knocks came up through the stand and then a held pause, like someone waiting at a door.
Here, nothing. Wet stone and a drip. My shoulders come down a whole inch. If Callista Veyne were up in that gallery tonight, my feet would give her nothing to watch.
Good. Wellhead's floor keeps its mouth shut. I can work.

We null two more before the Half. Dov Peals twice, the Lamplighter and a new one he christens the Wet Week, and bows to a gallery that doesn't clap. Grin Peals once for Wellhead with a long low note no pair could have touched, which goes through Marten and me for a weight each and still rings their side's point on our plate.
Two-one to us at the Half. At the Long Ground Marten hums his lullaby and I hum my one low note straight down, and there's nothing in either of us to clear.
"Pace five," says the Warden, for the second Half.

The floor's colder. I'd swear to it. The wet on the stands has gone from a fur to a film, and the bloom they beat up at the start sticks to my shins in a grey paste. Nobody else looks down. Nobody else has their feet on it.
The Drip's Raise. Lead-in through my soles: same pitch as his first. Same pair. I'd bet my banker on it.
"Marten. Drain side. Three. Two. Draw."
We draw. The front comes in, and comes in, and comes in, a hair later than it should, and then the note goes into me.
Not all of it. Half of it. The other half goes into Marten. My palms take it like a chisel taking a bad blow, a jar right up to the elbows, and my good ear starts to sing.
The Warden's rod goes to my stand. "Two held. Three, Halloway." To Marten's stand. "Two held. Thirty-seven, Sallow."
Marten waits until the Warden's mouth stops moving before he nods. "Aye, well," he says.

A doubling. Half a weight-three note each, rounded up: two held ring apiece, and a Mark apiece on the Book. Three for me now. Thirty-seven for Marten. An ordinary, Book-writing doubling, with a pair I'd have sworn was true. Banker's grief.

The front was late. I counted it against the tell-weight, the way I count everything: half a count later to my stand than the same note took in the first Half. I put that away in my head and I don't know what drawer it goes in.

Marten Grounds through the Breath, humming, and I feel his lullaby come up through my heels, low and steady. I don't hum. If I put my own note into the stone on top of his, I'll have two hums, a drip and no floor, and the floor's all I've got.
Dov throws. Wellhead's Dampers set early and take it between them. Still two-one.
"Drip's spent twenty-seven," says Sef in my right ear. "He's three left in him. He'll throw them all at once."

The Drip Raises. Pitch comes up through the stone, on our peg, near enough to Peal. A three, then, his last. There's a pair for it on the chart, Marten and the drain stand again, a hand's width further along.
Marten's looking at my mouth, waiting for my count.
I don't give it to him. I don't trust the pair, and I won't stand him in another bad one. He's at thirty-seven on the Book and he's never once asked me for anything.
"Off, Marten. Mine."
I step into the beam alone before the Raise ends, set my feet like bedding a stone and draw.
Three weight, into my palms, up my arms, into my teeth. My hands go out like lamps. There's a rush in my right ear like a river under a bridge.
"Five held," says the Warden. "Four, Halloway."
Five held. Hob Rennie's number. The last thing Hob did on a Drum floor was draw a five alone, holding five.
Sef is at my right shoulder before the Breath's half gone.
"Ground," he says. "Wren. Ground it."
"If I hum, I lose the floor."
"Then lose the floor."
"Then we lose the match."
"I'll call the Quiet."
"I'll stand in it with my mouth shut. Save it for something useful."
"Wren." He's never said my name twice in a row before. "Please. Hob was at five."
"I know what Hob was at."

He looks at me a long moment, at my hands hanging off my wrists like gloves. Then he turns to the floor and says, flat as a Warden: "Halloway's off. Every draw. Every throw. Marten, you don't move unless I say."

He's right. I know he's right, and I hate it like a cracked bed. At five my hands set half a count slow, and a Dead Air allows a tenth. If I called a pair now, Marten would draw on my count and I'd draw after it, and he'd take the whole note alone again, like at Ropewalk.
Dov Raises, voices, and bends his Widowmaker at the end, high and pretty and a semitone and a half wide of their peg. It rattles off Wellhead's plate like a spoon in a drawer.
"That was perfect," says Dov, to the whole Drum. "That was the finest Widowmaker ever thrown in a wet hole. The plate moved."
"Plates don't move without a Tuner," says Sef. "They haven't got one."

Dov doesn't answer that. He doesn't answer anything for a while. On his next throw he Raises a full count after Sef's call, and Wellhead's Dampers are set and waiting for him like cats at a mouse-hole.

Grin's Raise. I feel her pitch come up, and my head finds a pair before I can stop it, the old habit, and then the front comes in late again, crawling, and I feel the pair go wrong under my feet like a stone settling out of true.
"Off," I say, and don't move.
It goes through me and Marten for a weight each, still on pitch, and rings. Two-two.
Then two-three. Then a hard one from Grin, low and long, that no pair in the world could have nulled, and two-four.
"Wellhead, four," says the Warden. "Kilnyard, two."
Sef doesn't say three things. He says one. "Tannery top. Wellhead second. Us third."
They clear the Drum around me. Wellhead go up the stair laughing, and their gallery goes after them. Dov goes up last and doesn't look back, which for Dov is a speech.
I stay on my stand. I can't go up the stair holding five; I'd drop my own boots.
I plant my feet, heels then balls, the way I'd work a stone down into its bed, and I hum one low note straight down into the Wellhead floor.
At home, after Round One, humming into the floor felt like answering somebody. I stopped after a Breath. I couldn't do it.

Here it's like humming into a well. The note goes down and nothing comes back. Nothing waits. One Breath, four held. Two, three. By the fifth my fingers are closing and opening again, and nothing under this floor has so much as cleared its throat.
Then I do what I should have done before the first Raise.
I walk to the wall and knock it.

At home the slowstone rings dry and close. This wall rings dull, like knocking on a wet loaf. It's cold enough to ache my knuckle, and when I take my hand away there's a print in the sweat. The bloom's still hanging in the air, heavy with damp, settling on my lashes.
Cold and damp slow the pace. Everybody knows that. It's on the first page of the rulebook, and nobody reads the first page.

I draw in the wet bloom on the wall with one finger. The Drip's note. At pace five, call it two and six-tenths of a pace, crest to crest. Half that's a pace and three-tenths. That's the drain pair, true as a plumb line.
But the front was late. The pace had dropped. Say four and a half. Same note, now two and a third of a pace long. Half of that is a pace and a sixth.
Our pair's a pace and three-tenths. A hair over a tenth out.
A doubling.

The pair was never wrong. The floor moved under it. The spacing comes from the Drum as much as the note, and I've been reading the note and trusting the Drum like a fool trusting a lintel because it looked straight.
I'm a mason. I test the bed before I lay a stone. Every Drum from now on, I knock the walls before I take my boots off.

It's dark when we walk home. The cart left without us. Mrs. Oduya takes Marten's arm on the hill and pretends it's for her sake. Dov walks ahead with his hands in his pockets, still not talking. Sef walks on my right.
I'm working something through, and I don't tell him.
At home, in Round One, I held five ring on a Kilnyard stand and something under the floor answered me.
At home, in Round Three, barefoot, holding nothing, three knocks came up through the stand after a Dead Air.
Tonight I held five, barefoot, on a Wellhead stand. I nulled three clean ones before that. I Grounded five Breaths into this floor like a hand knocking on a door.
Nothing. Not a knock, not a hum, not a waiting silence.
At Ropewalk too, now I think back. Barefoot all night. I never thought to listen.
So it isn't the ring. It isn't my feet. It isn't me.
It's the floor.
Mrs. Oduya says our plates are cast for speaking. She won't say how she knows.
Whatever answered me doesn't live in my bones. It lives under the Kilnyard floor, or under floors like it, and I have no idea which other floors those are.
Callista Veyne might. On our stair she didn't say I'd heard something. She said I'd felt it. Nobody watches a mason's feet unless they know what a floor can do.
She knows something about our floor that I've only just worked out. And somebody sent her to watch me find it.
